newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghans flee fighting in northwestern province.
newsitem.headline: Afghans flee fighting in northwestern province.

text.p: Fierce fighting between the radical Islamic Taleban militia and its opponents has forced 40,000 to 50,000 Afghans to flee their homes in northwestern Afghanistan, a U.N. refugee agency said on Monday.

"Around 45,000 people from small towns and villages in front-line areas in Badghis province have fled southwards to the town of Qala-i-Nau," the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said in a statement. "Another 2,000 to 3,000 people have already proceeded further south to Herat.
The Taleban captured Herat, the main city in western Afghanistan, in September 1995.
A UNHCR spokesman, Rupert Colville, said 119 families, or about 800 people, had arrived in Herat in the last 24 hours.
"There are hundreds, if not thousands, of people pouring into Herat," Colville said, adding that it was the biggest displacement of people in western Afghanistan for many years.

He said a U.N. convoy of 22 trucks carrying tents, blankets and food had reached Qala-i-Nau, capital of Badghis province, on Monday and would begin distribution on Tuesday to 3,600 families (about 25,000 people) in Qala-i-Nau and other towns.
"It is not easy at all to get supplies up to Qala-i-Nau," he said. "The road is very bad and with fighting moving in a volatile fashion we may see further big movements southwards."
The UNHCR said many of the refugees were Koochi nomads, who live in black tents and wander with flocks of sheep and goats.
It quoted those arriving in Herat as speaking of heavy shelling and aerial bombardments, and said many had left their homes in such haste that they could not bring any belongings.
"Some of the women and children are reported to be in poor condition. Many of the Koochis have lost their livestock upon which their whole way of life depends," it said.
The Taleban have been locked in see-saw battles in Badghis with the combined forces of northern Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum and ousted government commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
The battle for Badghis, a relatively remote province, is important because success there for the Taleban could open up an invasion route into Dostum's northern heartland.
On the other hand, a Taleban defeat in Badghis could lay Herat open to attack by Dostum and allied forces loyal to the city's former governor Ismail Khan.

Khan, who fled to Iran when Herat fell to the Taleban, was reported last month to have sent hundreds of fighters in planes provided by Dostum to the town of Maimana in Faryab province, east of Badghis, to attack the Taleban.
Herat is populated mainly by Tajiks, the same ethnic group to which Masood and ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani belong. The Taleban draw most of their support from ethnic Pashtuns.
The UNHCR said that more than 9,000 displaced people were already concentrated in three areas of northern Afghanistan.

It said 15,000 Afghans, mostly from Kabul, had crossed into Pakistan since the start of October and 600 to 700 were arriving daily. "Many others may have left Kabul, unseen and uncounted, to stay with relatives elsewhere in the country," it said.
The UNHCR said 6,000 to 7,000 people had tried to escape the fighting in the northwest last week by fleeing into Turkmenistan, though many were since thought to have returned.

Afghans have constituted the world's biggest refugee population for the past 14 years. About 3.8 million have returned home since 1989, when the Soviet occupation ended, but more than a million remain in Pakistan and 1.4 million in Iran.
